danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: Inden felttogets begyndelse havde Rostov (Nikolaj) modtaget et brev fra sine forældre, hvori de kort fortalte om Natasjas sygdom og det brudte forlovelse med fyrst Andrej (hvilket de forklarede med, at Natasja havde afvist ham), og igen bad Nikolaj om at forlade hæren og vende hjem. Da Nikolaj modtog dette brev, forsøgte han ikke engang at få orlov eller afsked, men skrev til sine forældre, at han beklagede, at Natasja var syg og forlovelsen brudt, og at han ville gøre alt, hvad han kunne, for at opfylde deres ønsker. Til Sonja skrev han særskilt.

»Min sjæls elskede veninde!« skrev han. »Intet andet end æren kunne holde mig fra at vende hjem til landet. Men nu, ved felttogets begyndelse, ville jeg føle mig vanæret, ikke blot i mine kammeraters øjne, men i mine egne, hvis jeg foretrak min egen lykke frem for min kærlighed og pligt mod fædrelandet. Men dette skal blive vor sidste adskillelse. Tro mig, så snart krigen er forbi, hvis jeg stadig er i live og stadig elsket af dig, kaster jeg alt fra mig og flyver til dig for at trykke dig for evigt til mit brændende bryst.«

Det var i virkeligheden kun felttogets begyndelse, der forhindrede Rostov i at vende hjem, som han havde lovet, og gifte sig med Sonja. Efteråret i Otrádnoe med jagten og vinteren med julen og Sonjas kærlighed havde åbnet for ham et syn på rolige landlige glæder og fred, som han aldrig før havde kendt, og som nu lokkede ham. »En pragtfuld hustru, børn, en god hundemeute, et dusin kobler af smarte borzoi'er, landbrug, naboer, tjeneste ved valg...« tænkte han. Men nu begyndte felttoget, og han måtte blive ved sit regiment. Og da det nu engang måtte være sådan, følte Nikolaj Rostov sig, som det var naturligt for ham, tilfreds med livet i regimentet og formåede at finde glæde i det.

Ved sin hjemkomst fra orlov var Nikolaj blevet glædeligt modtaget af sine kammerater og sendt ud for at skaffe remonter, og han bragte fortræffelige heste hjem fra Ukraine, der glædede ham og indbragte ham ros fra sine overordnede. Under hans fravær var han blevet forfremmet til ritmester, og da regimentet blev sat på krigsfod med øget mandskab, fik han igen tildelt sin gamle eskadron.

Felttoget begyndte, regimentet rykkede ind i Polen med dobbelt sold, nye officerer ankom, nye mænd og heste, og frem for alt var alle gennemsyret af det muntert opstemte humør, der følger med et felttogs begyndelse, og Rostov, bevidst om sin fordelagtige stilling i regimentet, hengivet sig helt til fornøjelserne og interesserne i militærtjenesten, selv om han vidste, at han før eller senere ville måtte opgive dem.

Tropperne trak sig tilbage fra Vilna af forskellige indviklede statslige, politiske og strategiske grunde. Hvert skridt af tilbagetog var ledsaget af et indviklet spil af interesser, argumenter og lidenskaber i hovedkvarteret. For Pávlograd-husarerne var hele dette tilbagetog i den skønneste sommertid og med tilstrækkelige forsyninger imidlertid en meget enkel og behagelig sag.

Det var kun i hovedkvarteret, der herskede nedtrykthed, uro og intriger; i hærens krop spurgte man ikke sig selv, hvor man var på vej hen eller hvorfor. Hvis nogen beklagede at skulle trække sig tilbage, var det kun, fordi de måtte forlade kvarterer, de havde vænnet sig til, eller en køn ung polsk dame. Hvis tanken om, at det stod dårligt til, tilfældigvis faldt nogen ind, forsøgte han at være så munter, som det sømmer sig en god soldat, og ikke tænke på krigens generelle gang, men kun på den nærmeste opgave. Først slog de muntert lejr foran Vilna, stiftede bekendtskab med de polske godsejere, forberedte sig på parader og blev mønstret af kejseren og andre høje officerer. Så kom der ordre til at trække sig tilbage til Sventsyáni og ødelægge alle forsyninger, de ikke kunne medbringe. Sventsyáni blev husket af husarerne kun som den fulde lejr, et navn hele hæren gav deres ophold dér, og fordi der indkom mange klager over tropperne, der med henvisning til ordren om at indsamle forsyninger også tog heste, vogne og tæpper fra de polske godsejere. Rostov huskede Sventsyáni, fordi han den første dag efter ankomsten til den lille by skiftede sergentmajor og ikke kunne styre alle de fulde mænd i sin eskadron, der uden hans vidende havde tilegnet sig fem tønder gammelt øl. Fra Sventsyáni trak de sig længere og længere tilbage til Drissa og derfra endnu længere bag Drissa og nærmede sig grænsen til det egentlige Rusland.
Den trettende juli deltog Pávlograd-husarerne for første gang i en alvorlig træfning.
Den tolvte juli, aftenen før denne træfning, var der en voldsom storm med regn og hagl. Generelt var sommeren 1812 bemærkelsesværdig for sine storme.

De to Pávlograd-eskadroner bevogtede en rugmark, der allerede stod i aks, men var fuldstændig nedtrampet af kvæg og heste. Regnen faldt i strømme, og Rostov sad sammen med en ung officer ved navn Iljín, hans protegé, i et hastigt opført ly. En officer fra deres regiment med langt overskæg, der strakte sig ud over kinderne, og som efter at have redet til staben var blevet overrasket af regnen, trådte ind i Rostovs ly.
»Jeg kommer fra staben, greve. Har De hørt om Rajévskijs bedrift?«
Og officeren fortalte dem detaljerne om slaget ved Saltánov, som han havde hørt ved staben.

Rostov sad og røg sin pibe, drejede hovedet, mens vandet silede ned ad halsen, og lyttede uopmærksomt med et og andet blik til Iljín, der sad tæt op ad ham. Denne officer, en dreng på seksten, der for nylig var kommet til regimentet, stod nu i det samme forhold til Nikolaj, som Nikolaj havde stået i til Denisov syv år tidligere. Iljín forsøgte at efterligne Rostov i alt og tilbad ham, som en ung pige kunne have gjort.

Zdrsjínskij, officeren med det lange overskæg, fortalte svulstig om Saltánov-dæmningen som »et russisk Thermopylæ« og om, hvordan en bedrift værdig antikken var udført af general Rajévskij. Han fortalte, hvordan Rajévskij havde ført sine to sønner op på dæmningen under frygteligt ild og var stormet frem med dem ved sin side. Rostov hørte historien og sagde ikke blot intet for at opmuntre Zdrsjínskijs begejstring, men så tværtimod ud som en mand, der skammer sig over det, han hører, omend uden at ville modsige det. Siden felttogene ved Austerlitz og i 1807 vidste Rostov af erfaring, at folk altid lyver, når de fortæller om krigsbedrifter, som han selv havde gjort det, når han fortalte om sine; desuden havde han erfaring nok til at vide, at intet i krig sker, som vi kan forestille os eller berette det. Og derfor brød han sig ikke om Zdrsjínskijs beretning, ej heller om Zdrsjínskij selv, der med sit overskæg, der strakte sig over kinderne, bøjede sig lavt over tilhørerens ansigt, som det var hans vane, og trængte Rostov sammen i det snævre skur. Rostov så tavst på ham. »For det første må der have været en sådan forvirring og trængsel på dæmningen, der blev angrebet, at selv om Rajévskij førte sine sønner derop, kunne det højst have haft virkning på et dusin mænd tættest på ham,« tænkte han, »resten kunne ikke have set, hvordan eller med hvem Rajévskij kom op på dæmningen. Og selv de, der så det, ville ikke have ladet sig inspirere synderligt, for hvad havde de med Rajévskijs faderlige følelser at gøre, når deres eget skind var i fare? Og desuden afhang fædrelandets skæbne ikke af, om de indtog Saltánov-dæmningen eller ej, som vi fortælles var tilfældet ved Thermopylæ. Så hvorfor skulle han have bragt et sådant offer? Og hvorfor udsætte sine egne børn i slaget? Jeg ville ikke have taget min bror Petja med derop, eller engang Iljín, som er fremmed for mig men en rar fyr, men ville have forsøgt at anbringe dem et sted under dækning,« blev Nikolaj ved med at tænke, mens han lyttede til Zdrsjínskij. Men han gav ikke udtryk for sine tanker, for i sådanne sager havde han også opnået erfaring. Han vidste, at denne historie tjente til vore våbens ære, og man måtte altså lade, som om man ikke tvivlede på den. Og det gjorde han.

»Jeg kan ikke holde det ud mere,« sagde Iljín, der lagde mærke til, at Rostov ikke brød sig om Zdrsjínskijs samtale. »Mine strømper og min skjorte... og vandet løber under mig. Jeg går hen og finder ly. Regnen synes at tage af.«
Iljín gik ud, og Zdrsjínskij red bort.
Fem minutter senere kom Iljín sjaskende gennem mudderet løbende tilbage til skuret.

»Hurra! Rostov, kom hurtig! Jeg har fundet det! Omkring to hundrede meter herfra er der et værtshus, hvor vores allerede har samlet sig. Vi kan i det mindste komme til at tørre der, og Marja Hendríkhovna er der.«

Marja Hendríkhovna var regimentslægens kone, en køn ung tysk kvinde, han havde giftet sig med i Polen. Doktoren, hvad enten det skyldtes mangel på midler, eller fordi han ikke kunne lide at skilles fra sin unge hustru i de første dage af deres ægteskab, tog hende med sig overalt, hvor husarregimentet drog hen, og hans jalousi var blevet en stående vittighed blandt husarofficererne.

Rostov kastede kappen over skuldrene, råbte til Lavrúsjka, at han skulle følge med sagerne, og satte af sted med Iljín — nu glidende i mudderet, nu sjaskende lige igennem det — i den aftagende regn og det mørke, der af og til blev brudt af fjerne lyn.
»Rostov, hvor er du?«
»Her. Sikke et lyn!« råbte de til hinanden.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: Before the start of the campaign, Rostov had received a letter from his parents in which they told him briefly of Natasha's illness and the breaking off of her engagement to Prince Andrew (which they explained by saying that Natasha had rejected him), and again asked Nicholas to retire from the army and return home. On receiving this letter, Nicholas didn't even try to get leave or to retire, but wrote to his parents that he was sorry Natasha was ill and her engagement broken off, and that he would do all he could to meet their wishes. To Sonya he wrote separately.

"Adored friend of my soul!" he wrote. "Nothing but honor could keep me from returning to the country. But now, at the start of the campaign, I would feel dishonored — not only in my comrades' eyes but in my own — if I preferred my own happiness to my love and duty to the Fatherland. But this shall be our last separation. Believe me, as soon as the war is over, if I am still alive and still loved by you, I will throw up everything and fly to you, to press you forever to my loving heart."

It was in fact only the start of the campaign that prevented Rostov from returning home as he had promised and marrying Sonya. The autumn in Otradnoe with the hunting, and the winter with the Christmas holidays and Sonya's love, had opened up to him a vision of tranquil rural joys and peace such as he had never known before, and which now beckoned to him. "A wonderful wife, children, a good pack of hounds, a dozen leashes of swift borzois, farming, neighbors, elected public service..." he thought. But now the campaign was beginning, and he had to stay with his regiment. And since it had to be so, Nicholas Rostov, as was natural to him, found contentment in the life he led in the regiment and managed to find pleasure in it.

On his return from his leave, Nicholas was joyfully welcomed by his comrades and sent to buy remount horses. He brought back from Ukraine excellent horses that pleased him and earned him praise from his commanders. During his absence he had been promoted to captain, and when the regiment was put on a war footing with increased numbers, he was again given command of his old squadron.

The campaign began, the regiment was moved into Poland on double pay, new officers arrived, new men and horses, and above all everybody was infected with the merrily excited mood that goes with the start of a war. Rostov, conscious of his good standing in the regiment, devoted himself entirely to the pleasures and interests of military service, though he knew that sooner or later he would have to give them up.

The troops retreated from Vilna for various complicated reasons of state, political and strategic. Each step of the retreat was accompanied by a complex interplay of interests, arguments, and passions at headquarters. For the Pavlograd hussars, however, the whole retreat during the finest period of summer, with adequate supplies, was a very simple and pleasant affair.

It was only at headquarters that there was depression, uneasiness, and intrigue; in the body of the army no one asked where they were going or why. If they were sorry to retreat, it was only because they had to leave billets they had grown used to, or some pretty young Polish lady. If the thought that things looked bad happened to enter anyone's head, he tried to be as cheerful as befits a good soldier and not to think about the big picture, but only about the task nearest at hand. First they camped cheerfully near Vilna, making friends with the Polish landowners, preparing for reviews, and being reviewed by the Emperor and other high commanders. Then came an order to retreat to Sventsiany and destroy any supplies they couldn't carry. Sventsiany was remembered by the hussars only as "the drunken camp" — a name the whole army gave to their time there — because many complaints were made against the troops, who, using the order to collect supplies as cover, also took horses, carriages, and carpets from the Polish landowners. Rostov remembered Sventsiany because on the first day of their arrival in that small town he had to replace his sergeant major and was unable to manage all the drunken men of his squadron, who had secretly appropriated five barrels of old beer. From Sventsiany they retreated farther and farther to Drissa, and then beyond Drissa, drawing close to the Russian heartland.
On July thirteenth the Pavlograds took part in a serious engagement for the first time.
On the twelfth of July, the eve of that action, there was a violent storm of rain and hail. In general, the summer of 1812 was remarkable for its storms.

The two Pavlograd squadrons were camped in a field of rye, already in ear but completely trampled by cattle and horses. The rain was falling in torrents, and Rostov with a young officer named Ilyin, his protege, was sitting in a hastily built shelter. An officer of their regiment, with long mustaches extending onto his cheeks, who after riding to the staff had been caught by the rain, came into Rostov's shelter.
"I've come from the staff, Count. Have you heard about Raevsky's exploit?"
And the officer gave them details of the Saltanov battle, which he had heard at the staff.

Rostov, smoking his pipe and turning his head as the water trickled down his neck, listened with half an ear, with an occasional glance at Ilyin, who was pressing close beside him. This officer, a boy of sixteen who had recently joined the regiment, now stood in the same relation to Nicholas that Nicholas had been to Denisov seven years before. Ilyin tried to imitate Rostov in everything and adored him as a girl might have done.

Zdrzhinski, the officer with the long mustaches, spoke grandly of the Saltanov dam being "a Russian Thermopylae" and of how a deed worthy of antiquity had been performed by General Raevsky. He described how Raevsky had led his two sons onto the dam under terrific fire and had charged with them beside him. Rostov heard the story and not only said nothing to encourage Zdrzhinski's enthusiasm but, on the contrary, looked like a man ashamed of what he was hearing, though with no intention of contradicting it. Since the campaigns of Austerlitz and 1807, Rostov knew from experience that men always lie when describing military exploits, as he himself had done when telling them; besides, he had enough experience to know that nothing in war happens the way we can imagine or describe it. And so he didn't like Zdrzhinski's tale, nor did he like Zdrzhinski himself, who with his mustaches extending over his cheeks, leaned low over his listener's face as was his habit, crowding Rostov in the cramped shelter. Rostov looked at him in silence. "In the first place, there must have been such confusion and crowding on the dam being attacked that if Raevsky did lead his sons there, it could only have affected about a dozen men nearest to him," he thought. "The rest couldn't have seen who came onto the dam with Raevsky. And even those who did see wouldn't have been much inspired, because what did they care about Raevsky's tender paternal feelings when their own lives were at stake? And besides, the fate of the Fatherland didn't depend on whether they took the Saltanov dam or not, as we're told was the case at Thermopylae. So why would he have made such a sacrifice? And why bring his own children into battle? I wouldn't have brought my brother Petya there, or even Ilyin, who's a stranger to me but a nice lad — I would have tried to put them somewhere under cover," Nicholas continued to think as he listened to Zdrzhinski. But he didn't express his thoughts, for in such matters too he had learned from experience. He knew that this tale redounded to the glory of the Russian army and so one had to pretend not to doubt it. And he acted accordingly.

"I can't stand this any more," said Ilyin, noticing that Rostov didn't enjoy Zdrzhinski's conversation. "My stockings and shirt... and the water's running into my seat! I'll go look for shelter. The rain seems lighter."
Ilyin went out and Zdrzhinski rode away.
Five minutes later Ilyin, splashing through the mud, came running back to the shelter.
"Hurrah! Rostov, come quick! I've found it! About two hundred yards away there's a tavern where our fellows have already gathered. We can at least get dry there, and Mary Hendrikhovna's there."

Mary Hendrikhovna was the wife of the regimental doctor, a pretty young German woman he had married in Poland. The doctor, whether from lack of means or because he didn't like to be separated from his young wife in the early days of their marriage, took her along with him wherever the hussar regiment went, and his jealousy had become a standing joke among the hussar officers.

Rostov threw his cloak over his shoulders, shouted to Lavrushka to follow with the things, and — now slipping in the mud, now splashing right through it — set off with Ilyin in the lessening rain and the darkness that was occasionally torn by distant lightning.
"Rostov, where are you?"
"Here. What lightning!" they called to one another.
